overview.text: Soybean (Glycine max), also called soya, is an annual plant in the legume family, cultivated for its protein- and oil-rich seeds. Its leaves usually have three leaflets, and its roots can form nodules with bacteria that convert nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. People eat soybeans in many ways: young harvested beans are edamame, while processed beans are used for tofu, tempeh, soy drinks and other foods. Soybean oil is used in cooking and processed foods, and the protein-rich meal left after oil extraction is widely used in animal feed. Evidence suggests soybean was domesticated in China, though the precise history remains under study.

key_facts.text: Soybean is the cultivated species Glycine max in the Fabaceae, or legume, family; it is an annual crop.
Its foliage leaves are usually made up of three leaflets, and fine hairs can occur on the leaves, stems and pods.
Root nodules house bacteria that turn atmospheric nitrogen into a form available to plants; this helps explain why soybean is useful in crop rotations.
Edamame is soybean harvested as a vegetable while the pods are still green; mature soybeans are harvested as dry seeds.
Soybeans are processed into foods including tofu, tempeh, soy sauce and soy drinks; soybean oil and protein-rich meal also have major food and feed uses.
